text: Chapters 1 through 4 taught you imperative automation — PowerShell, Python, and CLI scripts that specify the steps to take, in order. This lesson introduces a different question entirely: not what steps do I run, but what should exist. That's declarative Infrastructure as Code, and it solves a real problem your scripts can't, no matter how carefully you write them.

New-AzStorageAccount is an instruction: create this, right now, with these settings. Run it twice and you either get an error because the account already exists, or, without a check you wrote yourself, a duplicate resource. The command has no memory of your intent — only the action you told it to take, once, this run.

A Bicep resource block describes the outcome instead: there should be a storage account, this name, this SKU, this region. Run it twice and nothing happens the second time, because the tool compares the declared state to what's already deployed and finds nothing left to reconcile. That's idempotency, built in as a default, not something you hand-code with an if-exists check.

Three real things declarative IaC gives you that a script doesn't: you describe the end state instead of the steps to reach it, every run is safe to repeat by default, and the tool can detect configuration drift — when something changed outside your automation entirely, and reality no longer matches what was declared.

Drift detection isn't theoretical. Azure's own az deployment group what-if command compares live resources against a declared template before you deploy anything, and reports exactly what changed. Terraform has the equivalent terraform plan. AWS CloudFormation has aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift. Each one answers the same question your scripts physically cannot: has reality moved while nobody was running the script?

Your Chapter 1-4 scripts aren't obsolete — plenty of real automation correctly stays imperative, and Chapter 6 comes back to exactly that kind of work. But drift detection is specifically a declarative capability. Next up: Azure's own native format for it, ARM templates, and the cleaner Bicep language Microsoft built that compiles down to them.
